title: English — Reading comprehension (200–250 words, vocabulary focus)

passages.title: Designing a Fair Experiment
passages.body:
When Priya noticed her bean plants leaning toward the classroom window, she wondered whether light direction affected growth. Instead of guessing, she designed a fair test. She planted twelve identical bean seeds in the same soil and watered them equally. Half the pots sat on a sunny windowsill; the other half rested under a grow lamp on the opposite wall. Every three days she measured stem height and recorded leaf colour in a notebook, sketching each plant so she could compare subtle changes.

Priya changed only the light source while keeping temperature and water constant. Her classmates suggested adding fertilizer to one group, but Priya refused because that would introduce a second variable. She also rotated the pots a quarter turn daily so stems would not lean toward one side only. After four weeks, the window group grew taller yet paler, while the lamp group stayed shorter but deep green. Priya concluded that both light intensity and direction mattered, and she presented bar graphs with error bars showing measurement ranges. Her teacher praised the careful controls and reminded the class that scientific conclusions remain tentative until others repeat the experiment under similar conditions. Priya posted her methods online so another school could try the same setup in a sunnier climate.

passages.title: Plastic Paths to the Sea
passages.body:
Plastic waste often begins on land long before it reaches the ocean. A discarded snack wrapper can slide into a storm drain during rain, travel through underground pipes, and eventually empty into a river. Wind may also tumble lightweight bags into creeks that feed larger waterways. Along the journey, sunlight and waves break bulky items into smaller fragments called microplastics, which persist for years because many plastics do not biodegrade quickly.

Marine animals sometimes mistake colourful bits for food. Seabirds feed plastic to chicks, and fish accumulate particles in their tissues. Scientists even find microplastics in remote Arctic ice, proving that ocean currents connect distant regions. Fishing gear lost at sea adds large, ghost nets that trap whales and turtles long after boats depart. Communities respond with bottle refunds, beach cleanups, and bans on single-use bags. Engineers design biodegradable packaging and improved recycling plants, yet reduction at the source remains the most direct solution. Students who audit their own lunch waste discover how daily habits contribute to a global problem that no single country can solve alone. Even small choices, like packing reusable containers or refusing straws, reduce the steady flow of plastic toward the sea and protect wildlife far from home.

passages.title: Why Sleep Matters for Learning
passages.body:
Sleep is not idle downtime; the brain actively reorganizes memories while the body rests. During deep sleep, the brain replays important events from the day, strengthening neural pathways that help you remember vocabulary, math procedures, and piano fingerings. Without adequate rest, attention drifts in class and new information slips away before it can be stored in long-term memory.

Teenagers often sacrifice sleep for screens or homework marathons, but chronic shortage can dull creativity and mood. The hormone melatonin signals nightfall, yet bright phone light can delay this cue, pushing bedtimes later and shortening the deepest sleep stages. Experts recommend consistent daily schedules, dark rooms, cool temperatures, and screen curfews before bed. Athletes notice slower reaction times after short nights, linking rest to physical performance as well as academics. Schools that start later report fewer tardy arrivals and better test focus, suggesting that schedules and health are linked. Parents and students who treat sleep as part of studying—not an enemy of it—often see steadier progress across subjects and fewer careless mistakes on quizzes. Keeping a simple sleep log for two weeks can reveal patterns—late caffeine, noisy rooms, or bright screens—that are easy to fix once they are clearly visible on paper.

passages.title: Urban Trees and Air Quality
passages.body:
City planners increasingly plant trees along streets and in pocket parks because urban forests deliver measurable benefits. Leaves absorb carbon dioxide during photosynthesis and intercept fine dust particles that would otherwise enter lungs. Shade from mature canopies lowers sidewalk temperatures in summer, reducing the urban heat island effect that makes downtown neighbourhoods hotter than surrounding farmland.

Tree roots also stabilize soil on slopes and soak up rainfall that might overwhelm storm sewers. Birds and insects use street trees as migration stopovers, adding biodiversity amid concrete. However, planting the wrong species in cramped tree wells can crack sidewalks or tangle with power lines. Arborists therefore select hardy native varieties, prune carefully, and monitor soil volume so roots have room to grow. Citizen volunteers who adopt young street trees—watering them through dry spells and mulching their bases—dramatically improve survival rates during the first fragile years. Municipal budgets may seem high for saplings, but long-term health savings from cleaner air and cooler blocks can offset costs. A single block may not transform regional air overnight, but many blocks together can make cities healthier places to breathe, walk, and play. Students who measure sidewalk temperature on tree-lined and bare streets can see the cooling effect with their own data.

questions.prompt: In the passage, "identical" most nearly means —
choices: the same in type and starting condition
different in every way
much larger than average
unable to grow
questions.answer: the same in type and starting condition

questions.prompt: Which word is the best antonym for "tentative" in the final sentence?
choices: uncertain
final and absolute
careful
repeated
questions.answer: final and absolute

questions.prompt: Why did Priya refuse to add fertilizer to only one group?
choices: It would add a second variable and ruin the fair test.
Fertilizer kills all bean plants instantly.
Her teacher banned notebooks in class.
The window group already had enough soil.
questions.answer: It would add a second variable and ruin the fair test.

questions.prompt: What can be inferred about the window group compared with the lamp group?
choices: They grew taller but paler, suggesting light direction and intensity both mattered.
They received no light at all during the experiment.
They were watered less often than the lamp group.
They were not measured during the four weeks.
questions.answer: They grew taller but paler, suggesting light direction and intensity both mattered.

questions.prompt: The teacher's final comment mainly emphasizes that strong conclusions require —
choices: repeated testing by others, not just one classroom trial
avoiding all measurements forever
changing many variables at once
ignoring graphs and numbers
questions.answer: repeated testing by others, not just one classroom trial

questions.prompt: In the passage, "accumulate" most nearly means —
choices: build up or collect over time
disappear instantly
float only on beaches
change into metal
questions.answer: build up or collect over time

questions.prompt: Which word is the best antonym for "biodegradable" as used for packaging?
choices: long-lasting in the environment
plant-based
recyclable
lightweight
questions.answer: long-lasting in the environment

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how do large plastic items become microplastics?
choices: Sunlight and waves break them into smaller fragments.
Fish chew them into identical spheres overnight.
Storm drains chemically dissolve them completely.
Recycling plants shrink them with magnets only.
questions.answer: Sunlight and waves break them into smaller fragments.

questions.prompt: Finding microplastics in Arctic ice suggests that —
choices: ocean currents can transport pollution to faraway regions
the Arctic has no wildlife
plastic only forms in tropical rivers
beach cleanups are useless everywhere
questions.answer: ocean currents can transport pollution to faraway regions

questions.prompt: The author states that reduction at the source is the most direct solution because —
choices: less waste entering the system prevents later harm downstream
engineers refuse to design new packaging
animals no longer eat any food in the ocean
storm drains have been removed from cities
questions.answer: less waste entering the system prevents later harm downstream

questions.prompt: In the passage, "chronic" most nearly means —
choices: continuing over a long period
happening once only
loud and musical
unrelated to health
questions.answer: continuing over a long period

questions.prompt: Which word is the best antonym for "adequate" as used to describe rest?
choices: insufficient
deep
organized
creative
questions.answer: insufficient

questions.prompt: What role does melatonin play according to the passage?
choices: It signals nightfall and helps prepare the body for sleep.
It strengthens arm muscles during sports.
It digests homework assignments in the stomach.
It blocks all memories from forming.
questions.answer: It signals nightfall and helps prepare the body for sleep.

questions.prompt: Bright phone light before bed can harm learning mainly by —
choices: delaying sleep cues and shortening restorative rest
increasing melatonin too early in the morning only
erasing all piano skills permanently in one night
making school start earlier every day
questions.answer: delaying sleep cues and shortening restorative rest

questions.prompt: The author's main point is that sleep —
choices: actively supports memory and school performance
is wasted time that slows learning
only matters for adults, not students
has no connection to mood or creativity
questions.answer: actively supports memory and school performance

questions.prompt: In the passage, "intercept" most nearly means —
choices: catch or block before passing through
plant in cramped soil
melt during winter
shine brighter at night
questions.answer: catch or block before passing through

questions.prompt: Which word is the best antonym for "hardy" as used for tree species?
choices: delicate and easily damaged
native
shady
tall
questions.answer: delicate and easily damaged

questions.prompt: What is the urban heat island effect?
choices: Downtown areas become hotter than nearby rural land.
Trees remove all carbon dioxide instantly.
Sidewalks freeze earlier than forests in summer.
Rainfall stops completely in cities.
questions.answer: Downtown areas become hotter than nearby rural land.

questions.prompt: Why do arborists prefer native hardy varieties in cramped tree wells?
choices: They are less likely to damage sidewalks or fail in local conditions.
They never need water during droughts.
They grow only underground without leaves.
They block all dust permanently with one sapling.
questions.answer: They are less likely to damage sidewalks or fail in local conditions.

questions.prompt: The author ends by suggesting that city health improves when —
choices: many neighbourhoods together plant and care for trees
citizens remove all street trees to cool sidewalks
volunteers stop watering young trees during dry spells
planners choose only the largest exotic species
questions.answer: many neighbourhoods together plant and care for trees
